short: The OMB memorandum governing federal agency AI adoption. Compliance plans, Chief AI Officers, public use case inventories, and high-impact determinations.
title: OMB M-25-21 and Federal Agency AI Governance
subtitle: Compliance plans, Chief AI Officers, use case inventories, high-impact AI
body_html:
On this page

  • What M-25-21 requires
  • The other half: M-25-22 on acquisition
  • A worked example: the CFPB plan
  • A second example: the SEC
  • A third example: HHS at scale
  • What the inventories actually show
  • Why this reaches private companies
  • What to do if you sell to an agency

The one-paragraph answer

OMB Memorandum M-25-21, Accelerating Federal Use of AI through Innovation, Governance, and Public Trust, issued April 3, 2025, is the rulebook for how federal agencies adopt AI, and its companion M-25-22 governs how they buy it. Each agency must publish a compliance plan, name a Chief AI Officer, stand up an AI governance body, maintain an AI use case inventory that is submitted to OMB and published in part, and apply extra scrutiny to high-impact AI. It binds agencies rather than companies, but it reaches any company that sells software to the government, because an agency cannot deploy what it cannot inventory, assess and authorise.

What M-25-21 requires

The memorandum sits alongside the AI in Government Act of 2020 and the Advancing American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2022. Agency compliance plans published under it share a common spine.

  • A Chief AI Officer. A named official accountable for AI governance, innovation and compliance across the agency. Smaller agencies commonly combine the role with the Chief Information Officer.
  • An AI governance body. A cross-functional group with authority to review and approve AI use cases, typically drawing in IT, acquisition, legal, cybersecurity, privacy and civil rights.
  • An AI use case inventory. A central record of every planned and existing AI use, expressly including AI embedded in commercial software the agency merely bought. Submitted to OMB, with a public version posted.
  • High-impact determinations. Each use case is tested against the memorandum’s high-impact criteria, with AI impact assessments required for those that qualify.
  • Authority to operate, and the power to stop. AI must be authorised before deployment, and use that fails minimum safeguards is suspended pending remediation.

What the inventories actually show

The inventories are the part of this memorandum that produces evidence rather than intention, and the Department of Justice inventory is the one to read. It lists 314 AI use cases, none withheld from public reporting, and DOJ itself marks 114 of them high-impact. Against the seven minimum risk-management practices M-25-21 requires for high-impact AI, not one of those 114 records a completed practice.

The full breakdown is here, with the counts traceable to the published file. It is worth reading beside the April 3, 2026 deadline above.

The other half: M-25-22 on acquisition

OMB issued two memoranda on April 3, 2025, and agency plans treat them as a pair. M-25-21 governs how an agency uses AI. M-25-22, Driving Efficient Acquisition of Artificial Intelligence in Government, governs how it buys AI. If you sell software, the second one is the one that reaches you.

The HHS strategy is unusually specific about what that means at the contract level. It says cross-functional teams including contracting, technical, legal, privacy and civil rights experts will plan procurements; that solicitations will strongly encourage model auditability, transparency, and clear data and intellectual property rights; and that contracts will avoid vendor lock-in through open and portable solutions and will bar any use of HHS data to train separate models without explicit consent.

Read that last clause twice if your product improves from customer data. It is becoming a contract term, not a policy preference.

A worked example: the CFPB plan

The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau published its plan on September 26, 2025, signed by Chris Chilbert as Chief Information Officer and Acting Chief AI Officer. It is short, candid, and more useful than a longer document would be, because it says what the agency cannot do as well as what it can.

The Bureau states that its AI adoption is limited in scope and scale, and that its innovation strategy prioritises low-risk, incremental use in mission support and administrative functions: document classification, internal workflows, limited data analysis. It names its constraints plainly, citing limited technical, legal, cybersecurity and privacy resources for vetting AI use cases, and says it is addressing them by working with the Small Agency CIO and CISO Councils and by leaning on federal shared services and FedRAMP-authorised tools.

Two details are worth copying into a private-sector programme. Where the agency lacks source access to a proprietary model, it says it will fall back on output monitoring and vendor attestations rather than treating the gap as unreviewable. And to catch AI that programme offices never reported, or never realised was AI, its Office of Cybersecurity monitors IT activity using the same approach it uses to discover shadow IT. Most enterprises have the same blind spot and no equivalent control.

A second example: the SEC

The Securities and Exchange Commission announced an agency-wide AI Task Force on August 1, 2025, led by Valerie Szczepanik as Chief AI Officer, under Chairman Paul S. Atkins. The stated purpose is internal: centralising AI efforts across divisions, removing barriers, and maintaining governance across the AI lifecycle. The SEC reported 30 AI use cases in its 2024 inventory, including extracting information from securities filings, identifying potentially manipulative trading, and reviewing public comments.

The contrast with the CFPB is instructive. Both are financial regulators under the same memorandum. One is building enterprise AI capacity with a dedicated task force; the other is deliberately staying small and buying rather than building. Both approaches comply.

A third example: HHS at scale

The Department of Health and Human Services published both a compliance plan and a full AI Strategy on September 30, 2025, issued by Deputy Secretary Jim O’Neill and Acting Chief AI Officer Clark Minor, who is also the Department’s Chief Information Officer. If the CFPB shows what a small agency does under this memorandum, HHS shows what a very large one does.

The numbers are the story. HHS reported 271 AI use cases in FY2024 across the Department, and the strategy projects roughly 70% growth for FY25 based on the inventory then in development. Its AI Governance Board is chaired by the Deputy Secretary, includes Division leadership, and meets at least twice a year. The Department states that it made ChatGPT available to every employee, and says it led the federal government in doing so.

The deadline is the part worth copying into a calendar. The HHS plan states that by April 3, 2026, all Divisions will apply the minimum risk management practices in M-25-21 to high-impact AI, and that Divisions unable to meet the deadline will stop the applicable AI tool until they achieve compliance. It adds that before that date, HHS may ask third-party contractors and vendors to voluntarily take action such as providing updated documentation or testing measures.

So a vendor whose high-impact product cannot evidence testing by that date is not facing a strongly worded letter. It is facing a stop.

Why this reaches private companies

M-25-21 imposes no duty on a private company. It changes what agencies can buy, which is a duty in everything but name.

An agency must inventory AI embedded in commercial software. That means a customer will ask you to declare AI features you may not currently document, including ones added in a routine release. It must make a high-impact determination, which requires knowing what the model does and what decision it influences. Where it cannot inspect a proprietary model, it will ask for vendor attestations, and someone at your company will have to sign one. And it must be able to suspend a non-compliant use, which makes an undisclosed AI feature a contract risk rather than a product surprise.

The federal market is also a leading indicator. Procurement language written for agencies under this memorandum tends to appear in large enterprise contracts a year or two later.

What to do if you sell to an agency

  1. Write down where the AI is. Every model in the product, what it does, what data it touches, and whether it is yours or a subprocessor’s. You will be asked, and a vague answer reads as an undisclosed capability.
  2. Decide what you will attest to. Vendor attestations are the agency’s fallback when it cannot see inside the model. Work out in advance what your organisation can truthfully sign, and who signs it.
  3. Make AI changes announceable. If a release adds or materially changes a model, the customer’s inventory is now stale and their authorisation may not cover it. Build the notification into your release process rather than the account team’s inbox.
  4. Support monitoring you cannot provide access for. If you will not expose the model, expose the outputs: logs, decision records, and enough evidence for someone else to evaluate behaviour from the outside.

Frequently asked questions

Does M-25-21 apply to my company?

Not directly. It binds federal agencies. It reaches you through what your agency customer must be able to say about your product.

Where can I read an agency’s AI use case inventory?

Agencies submit inventories to OMB and post a public version on their own websites, in accordance with the Advancing American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2022 and OMB guidance. Coverage and format vary by agency.

What counts as high impact?

The criteria are set out in the memorandum itself. As a practical baseline, agencies have said they will scrutinise any AI used in programme decisions, public interactions, or oversight activities.

How does this relate to the NIST AI Risk Management Framework?

The framework is referenced by agency plans as a source of practice rather than as a binding requirement. M-25-21 sets the governance obligations; NIST supplies much of the method.

Primary sources

The documents behind this summary. Where a compliance decision turns on exact wording, read the source rather than this page.

  • SEC press release 2025-103, SEC Creates Task Force to Tap Artificial Intelligence for Enhanced Innovation and Efficiency Across the Agency, August 1, 2025.
  • AI in Government Act of 2020; Advancing American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2022.
  • NIST AI Risk Management Framework
